questions.question: A sentence/a part of the sentence is underlined. Four alternatives are given to the underlined part which will improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative and click the button corresponding to it. In case no improvement is needed, click the button corresponding to "No improvement". Is there any way we can reschedule the appointment at Tuesday ?
questions.questionHtml:
A sentence/a part of the sentence is underlined. Four alternatives are given to the underlined part which will improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative and click the button corresponding to it. In case no improvement is needed, click the button corresponding to "No improvement".

Is there any way we can reschedule the appointment at Tuesday?
questions.solution: 'At' is not used to refer to days (on should have been used instead). 'In' means inside something, which is not grammatically correct to use with days of a week. 'With' means accompanied by. A day cannot accompany something. 'For Tuesday' means that the appointment is to be held on Tuesday. This is grammatically correct, making C the right answer.

questions.question: Select the option that can substitute the underlined word in the given idiom. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'. A taste of your own drink .

questions.solution:
The given idiom is "A taste of your own drink." The underlined word here is "drink", which needs to be replaced by the word 'medicine'.

The idiom "A taste of your own medicine" means experiencing the same harmful or unpleasant thing that one has been doing to others. It's a metaphorical way of saying that someone is being treated the way they have treated others.

Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Sapna and Suman (was best friends) at the start of the session but now they have grown to be rivals.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully.

Sapna and Suman (was best friends) at the start of the session but now they have grown to be rivals.
questions.solution: The correct option that completes the sentence is (a). In the original sentence, 'Sapna and Suman' is a plural subject, so the verb that follows should be in the plural form to agree with the subject. 'Were' is the correct past tense plural form of the verb 'to be' for the subject 'Sapna and Suman'. Option (b) does not accurately represent the past tense of the verb and does not fit the context of the sentence. Option (c) is in the future tense and does not accurately reflect the past tense of the verb needed for this sentence. Option (d) is not the appropriate verb form for the plural subject and is also not in the correct tense. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Select the alternative that will improve the underlined part of the sentence. In case there is no improvement required, select 'No improvement'. Me and Daksha are planning to start a company.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the alternative that will improve the underlined part of the sentence. In case there is no improvement required, select 'No improvement'.

Me and Daksha are planning to start a company.
questions.solution:
Here, the error in the underlined part is that 'me' is an object pronoun and is used as a subject pronoun. A similar mistake is made in option (c) i.e. using the subject pronoun instead of the object pronoun or vice versa.

Whenever two pronouns are used as subjects, the second/third-person pronoun (He/she/they/you) precedes the 'first' person pronoun (I/We) in a positive sentence.

Hence, (b) is correct.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. He usually sits besides Vicky in class.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

He usually sits besides Vicky in class.
questions.solution:
The meaning of the word 'besides' is 'in addition to' or 'apart from'. The sentence is about a person who sits regularly at a place and that place is described with respect to the position of Vicky. The correct word to denote the position is 'beside' which means 'at the side of' or 'next to'. Options b) and d) are eliminated because of the incorrect usage of the word 'besides'. Option c) is eliminated because it is incomplete. The present participle verb 'sitting' requires the auxiliary verb 'is' before it to form the correct tense structure of the present continuous tense.

From the given options, the one that is in the correct form is option (a) 'sits beside'.

Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

Note:-

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. Personal growth (transforming) lives profoundly.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

Personal growth (transforming) lives profoundly.
questions.solution:
'Transforming' (-ing form of verb) requires a helping verb before it which is absent in the given sentence.

Options (a) and (b) are incorrect as the verb following the helping verbs 'was' and 'is' should either be a past participle (V3) or a present participle verb (V4, i.e., the -ing form of the verb), but 'transform' is a base verb.

Option (d) is incorrect as it incorrectly uses the plural verb 'are' for the singular subject 'personal growth'.

Option (c) correctly uses the singular present tense verb "transforms," which agrees with the singular subject "personal growth." This choice effectively conveys the idea that personal growth is an ongoing process that has a profound impact on lives. It is the most suitable choice as it maintains subject-verb agreement. Hence, (c) is the correct answer.

The final sentence: Personal growth transforms lives profoundly.

The rest of the options form grammatically incorrect sentences.

Note: Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

A participle is a word derived from a verb that can be used as an adjective or to form certain verb tenses. There are two main types of participles:

Past participles (typically ending in -ed, -en, -n, -ne, or -t) are used for perfect tenses and passive voice constructions.

Present participles (always ending in -ing) are used for continuous tenses.

questions.question: Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. When the escaped convict (were apprehended by the authorities), he was hiding in an abandoned warehouse.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully.

When the escaped convict (were apprehended by the authorities), he was hiding in an abandoned warehouse.
questions.solution:
The correct option that completes the sentence is (a). The original sentence is in the past tense, indicated by the word 'was' before the verb 'hiding'. Therefore, the correct form of the verb should also be in the past tense. 'Was apprehended' is the correct past tense form of the verb 'apprehend' for the third-person singular subject 'the escaped convict'. The other options do not provide the correct verb form or subject-verb agreement. Option (b) uses the present tense 'is apprehended' instead of the correct past tense 'was apprehended'. Option (c) does not use the correct past tense form of the verb 'apprehend'. Option (d) uses the present tense 'are apprehended' instead of the correct past tense 'was apprehended'. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Subject-verb agreement means that a subject and its verb must be both singular or both plural:

A singular subject takes a singular verb.

A plural subject takes a plural verb.

For example, in the sentence 'John lives in France', the subject John (singular 'he') 'agrees with' the third person singular form of the verb to live - lives.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'. I played a paradox on my sister by hiding fake spiders in her room.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.

I played a paradox on my sister by hiding fake spiders in her room.
questions.solution:
The word "paradox" doesn't accurately convey the intended meaning in the context of the sentence. A "paradox" is a concept or statement that seems contradictory or goes against common belief, yet it might be true or logical within a specific context. In contrast, the sentence implies that the speaker played a trick or a practical joke on his/her sister by hiding fake spiders in her room. This action aligns more with the concept of a "prank" rather than a "paradox." A prank involves a playful or mischievous act intended to trick, amuse, or surprise someone, typically in a light-hearted manner. Accordingly, 'prank' is a suitable word to replace 'paradox'. 'Foul' refers to something that is offensive, unpleasant, or morally unacceptable. However, in the context of the sentence, the act of hiding fake spiders as a joke on the sister doesn't necessarily imply anything offensive or morally wrong. Therefore, "foul" doesn't appropriately replace "paradox" in this context. A 'riddle' is a type of puzzle or enigmatic question that requires thought or cleverness to solve. However, the sentence is describing an action, not a puzzle or a question posed to someone. So, "riddle" isn't the appropriate replacement for "paradox" in this context. Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

The revised sentence is: I played a prank on my sister by hiding fake spiders in her room.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'. The thunder roared broadly during the storm.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.

The thunder roared broadly during the storm.
questions.solution:
In the sentence "The thunder roared broadly during the storm," the word "broadly" (generally or inclusively) is used to describe how the thunder roared. However, "broadly" is not the most suitable adverb to convey the sound of thunder during a storm. The word "loudly" is the most appropriate substitution for "broadly" in this context. "Loudly" more accurately describes the nature of thunder during a storm, indicating that the thunder produced a strong, powerful sound that could be heard over a wide area. The word "patiently" means to act with patience or tolerance, especially in dealing with delays or difficulties. However, in the context of the sentence describing thunder during a storm, "patiently" does not appropriately convey the nature of the sound or the manner in which the thunder roared. "Sensibly" means acting with good judgment or practicality. This word also doesn't accurately describe the sound or manner of the thunder during the storm. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

The revised sentence is: The thunder roared loudly during the storm.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Rita is the shorter in the entire school.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Rita is the shorter in the entire school.
questions.solution:
The sentence compares Rita with everyone else at the school.

The sentence has used the article 'the', which is used before superlative degree. Also, the phrase 'entire school' indicates that more than two people have been compared.

Therefore, the comparative adjectives do not fit here, which makes options a) and d) incorrect. Thus, a substitution is required. Option b) is contextually incorrect as it does not meaningfully qualify the noun 'Rita'. It should be noted that height is not qualified using the adjective 'long'. Option c) is in superlative degree.

Therefore, the correct answer is option c).

Note:

The Positive Degree of an Adjective is the Adjective in its simple form. It is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

The Comparative degree of an adjective denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of the quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

Definite and indefinite articles: In English language, we have one definite article 'the'; it refers to, or introduces, a particular, specific noun. 'An' and 'a' are indefinite articles; they refer to, or introduce, an unspecified noun.
